Robust metamodel-based simulation-optimization approaches for designing
hybrid renewable energy systems
Pardis Pourmohammadi, Ahmed Saif ∗
Department of Industrial Engineering, Dalhousie University, 5269 Morris Street, Halifax, B3J 1B6, NS, Canada
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Hybrid renewable energy systems
Distributionally robust optimization
Simulation-optimization
Response surface methodology
A B S T R A C T
We propose two robust metamodel-based approaches for designing stand-alone hybrid renewable energy
systems that combine conventional and renewable energy generators with battery storage. Since the cost
and reliability functions of the stochastic system do not have closed-form expressions, they can only be
estimated via simulation. In the response surface methodology , the simulation input/output data is used first
to locally fit first-degree surrogate functions for each supply scenario to perform a stochastic gradient descent,
before a second-degree function is fitted and optimized when the gradient becomes small. In contrast,
the global response surface technique globally fits a convex quadratic surrogate function on the simulation
input/output data, then uses its minimizer to iteratively refine the search space. To account for estimation
errors, a distributional ambiguity set based on a linear 𝜙-divergence function is constructed around the
nominal probability distribution of supply scenarios, and the expected reliability-adjusted cost of the system is
computed using the worst-case distribution in this set. The validity of the proposed approaches and the value
of considering distributional ambiguity are demonstrated through a realistic case study of a remote community
in Northern Ontario.
1. Introduction
With the steady growth in global energy demand and the rising
concerns over environmental change, pollution, and depletion of fossil
energy resources, renewable energy sources (RES) like solar and wind
are posed to play a key role in our transition to a sustainable econ-
omy [1,2]. Stand-alone hybrid renewable energy systems (HRES) that
combine locally available RES with conventional energy generation
and/or energy storage technologies constitute a viable alternative for
serving the energy requirements of remote and isolated communities
when their connection to centralized power grids is not technically
and/or economically feasible [ 3]. However, given the intermittent
nature of RES and the high cost of large-scale energy storage, it is
crucial that the design of HRES is optimized so they can deliver
energy economically and reliably. Therefore, the problem of optimal
design of HRES has received a considerable attention from the scientific
community in the last two decades [ 4–8].
Simulation–optimization (SO) is a widely-used method for HRES
planning [9]. SO is particularly suitable when the problem’s objective
and/or constraint functions are difficult to express explicitly (analyti-
cally), but can be evaluated in a black-box model through simulation
for a particular input [ 10]. Generally speaking, SO approaches can
be categorized into model-based and metamodel-based methods [ 11].

Model-based SO encompasses ranking and selection, gradient search
methods ( i.e., stochastic optimization), direct (derivative-free) search
methods and random/heuristic search methods like genetic algorithms
(GA), simulated annealing (SA) and tabu search (TS) [ 10]. On the
other hand, metamodel-based or surrogate models approximate the
unknown input/output relationship of the system using an easy-to-
optimize function [12]. Response surface, Kriging and neural network
methods are among the most widely-used metamodels [ 13].
Given the stochastic, nonlinear and dynamic nature of HRES op-
erations, metamodel-based SO represents a promising framework for
planning them [ 14]. However, the literature on HRES design using
metamodels in general, and response surface methods (RSM) in par-
ticular, is still sparse. Ekren and Ekren [ 15] used RSM to optimally
size an autonomous solar/wind HRES with battery storage by min-
imizing the system cost and loss of load probability (LLP). Subse-
quently, Ekren et al. [ 16] conducted a break-even analysis and com-
pared a grid-connected system to a stand-alone system in terms of their
net present values using a similar RSM. Ren et al. [ 17] presented a
simulation-based strategy for optimal design of a renewable cooling
and heating system, and devised a solution approach that integrates
an integer-based GA with RSM.

A key limitation of SO methods in the context of stochastic systems
is that they require the probability distribution (or the underlying data-
generating process) of the simulation inputs to be known with certainty,
otherwise the solutions obtained might be sub-optimal [18]. In this
sense, they are quite similar to sample average approximation (SAA)
methods that are known to have poor out-of-sample performance,
especially when based on small data samples [19], which is often the
case in HRES planning. To reduce the sensitivity of SO models to the
simulation parameters and to hedge against uncertainty about them,
a robust approach was investigated by Dellino et al. [18,20]. Their
proposed approach adopts Taguchi’s view of the uncertain world, but
replaces its statistical techniques to tackle robustness using metamodels
by Kriging and RSM.
A less-conservative approach for dealing with parameter uncertainty
that has gained significant interest recently is distributionally-robust
optimization (DRO) [21]. In DRO, the expected value of a probabilistic
cost function is optimized, where the expectation is taken with respect
to the worst-case probability distribution from a distributional ambigu-
ity set (DAS) that is constructed based on historical data or parametric
information about the ‘‘true’’ distribution. Although DRO has found
application in some energy optimization studies [22–24], DRO models
used so far are based on explicit formulations that require the objective
and constraint functions to be fully known, which is not the case in
HRES design problems.
Although SO is the most commonly-applied approach to design
HRES, the vast majority of SO models use metaheuristics that often fall
into local optima and require excessive numbers of simulation evalua-
tions [25,26]. Metamodel-based approaches are shown to outperform
metaheuristics, especially for complex problems [27]. However, among
the handful of studies that apply metamodel-based SO in the context of
HRES design, e.g., [15,17], the issue of distributional ambiguity, arising
when few supply and demand scenarios extracted from limited data
are used in the simulation, is largely ignored, leading to HRES designs
that perform sub-optimally in reality. On the other hand, classical
DRO models that can alleviate this issue are based on canonical-form
optimization ( i.e., explicit objective function and constraints) and are
not suited for SO methods. The current paper fills this research gap by
showing how metamodel-based SO methods can be embedded in a DRO
framework to provide robust HRES designs that significantly outper-
form designs based on classical methods that directly use the empirical
probability distribution of scenarios. In particular, the contribution
of this paper is twofold. First, it provides novel and generic design
approaches that combine RSM and DRO to overcome the limitations of
existing methods. Second, it demonstrates the superiority of the robust
designs obtained using the proposed approaches through extensive
numerical analysis.
We propose two novel approaches for robustly optimizing the design
of HRES under ambiguity about the probability distribution of solar
and wind energy supply scenarios. Since the objective function can
be evaluated only through simulation, response surface metamodels
are fitted on the input/output (I/O) simulation data using design of
experiments (DoE) techniques. The first approach uses a classical RSM
that locally approximates the response function and uses gradient infor-
mation and a line search to update the best design, before performing
and optimizing a second-order approximation in the last iteration.
The second approach, in contrast, globally approximates the response
function and optimizes the convex quadratic approximation by solving
a DRO problem to refine the search space in each iteration until
the algorithm converges to an optimal design. To model uncertainty
in both cases, first, a manageable number of solar and wind supply
scenarios are generated from raw data using 𝑘-means clustering, and
their probabilities are estimated and used to generate an empirical
distribution. Then, a 𝜙-divergence ambiguity set is constructed around
the empirical distribution of scenarios to account for estimation errors.
The two proposed approaches are applied to a hypothetical (yet re-
alistic) case study that entails designing a solar–wind–battery–diesel
HRES for an isolated community in Canada. Comparisons between the
two approaches are conducted for both the nominal and the robust
problems.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. The next section
describes the HRES to be optimized and presents the mathematical
formulation of its optimal design problem. Section 3 presents the 𝑘-
means clustering method used to extract supply scenarios and the
𝜙-divergence ambiguity set constructed based on their empirical dis-
tribution. Section 4 explains, in detail, the two approaches proposed
to robustly designing a HRES: the classical RSM and the global response
surface technique (GRST). The regression models used to fit the I/O data
in each approach are presented in the same section, along with the
way distributional ambiguity is incorporated into the design process. In
Section 5, the numerical results obtained from applying the proposed
approaches on a realistic case study are compared and thoroughly an-
alyzed. Finally, conclusions and ideas for future research are provided
in Section 6.
2. System description and problem formulation
This section provides a brief description of the system under con-
sideration, including its operational rules. Then, it presents the no-
tations used to formulate the HRES design problem, along with the
mathematical formulation of the objective functions and constraints.
2.1. The HRES and its operational rules
The HRES of interest consists of photovoltaic panels (PV), wind
turbines (WT), a battery bank (BB) and a diesel generator (DG). We
assume that the types and characteristics of these system components
are pre-selected by the planner based on the location of the system
and the available technologies, whereas their numbers/capacities are
to be determined by solving an optimization problem. Since the re-
mote/isolated community to be served is not connected to the grid,
it has to rely on available local resources to satisfy its energy demand.
This is to be achieved while minimizing the annualized total cost of
the system, which includes both the capacity cost of its components,
amortized over their useful lives, and the expected annual cost of fuel
consumed by the DG. Power outputs of the PV and WT are intermit-
tent and unpredictable since they depend on meteorological variables
(e.g., solar irradiance, wind speed, temperature), but the planner has
access to some historical output data for both. On the other hand,
and without loss of generality, we assume that the total demand for
energy in each period ( e.g., hour) of the year can be predicted with
high accuracy. If this assumption does not hold, one can simply treat
the stochastic demand in the same way PV and WT outputs are treated,
as will be explained later. All generation and storage units, along with
the load, are assumed to be connected to the same bus, i.e., power flow
losses are ignored. This is a reasonable assumption for small-scale HRES
typically used in remote communities.
HRES are usually operated according to preset rules that specify, for
example, which energy source is to be utilized when there is a mismatch
between RES supply and demand. The utilization priority of the system
resources is illustrated in Fig. 1. Based on this priority, the operational
rules of the system are described as follows: In any time interval, if
demand exceeds the energy supplied by the renewable generators (PV
& WT), the shortage is compensated by the BB within its discharge rate
and energy limits. The remaining demand (if any) is met by the DG
within its rated capacity, then any excess loads are curtailed. On the
other hand, if the energy supplied by the renewable generators exceeds
demand, the excess energy is used to charge the BB within its charge
rate and energy limits, then any remaining energy is dumped. There
rules ensure that the BB is never charged directly from the DG, that
load curtailment happens only when all sources (WT, PV, BB & DG) are
not enough to satisfy the demand, and that energy cannot be dumped
if the demand is yet to be fully satisfied.

3. Modeling uncertainty
The mathematical model presented in the previous section treats
PV and WT outputs as deterministic parameters. In realty, however,
these are time-series data characterized by high variability, uncertainty
and auto-correlation [30]. To capture these characteristics, and given
the daily cyclic nature of RES supply data, one can simply consider
each available supply sample ( i.e., day) as a ‘‘scenario’’ and optimize
the expected objective value, where the expectation is taken with
respect to the distribution of supply scenarios. However, the problem
becomes computationally expensive when the number of scenarios is
large, which calls for scenario reduction techniques to be applied.
Hence, we use 𝑘-means clustering to extract a manageable number of
supply scenarios that can reasonably model parameter variability while
maintaining tractability. Furthermore, Since the probability distribu-
tion of the extracted scenarios is based a relatively small number of
sample points, it can significantly deviate from the true distribution.
Thus, we employ a robust approach to hedge the HRES design against
distributional ambiguity. A brief description of the DAS utilized for this
purpose is provided later.

the empirical distribution, the number of scenarios, and the desired
confidence level. This optimal value can be determined through cross-
validation, by which the solutions obtained using different 𝜌 values
are simulated on new ( i.e., out-of-sample) data and the 𝜌 value corre-

cross-validation method used to properly size the DAS is explained in
more detail and implemented in Sections 5.2 and 5.3.
4. Solution methods
Unlike the deterministic model where explicit functions exist to
evaluate TAC and LLP under simplifying assumptions, such closed-form
expressions do not exist for the real-case ( i.e., with real RES supply
data). Instead, these objectives have to be estimated using simulation
and optimized in a SO framework. In what follows, we present two
metamodel-based SO approaches that successively approximate the
complex I/O surface of the simulation model using easy-to-optimize
surrogate functions and show how to deal with distributional ambiguity
in both.

Daily PV and WT supply scenarios are generated from historical

We first note that the two methods led to substantially different
solutions in all cases, with relative differences in component num-
bers/capacities ranging between 1.7% and 26.5%. However, the rel-
ative differences in TAC and reliability between the optimal designs
obtained from the two methods are much smaller, not exceeding 0.3%
and 1.2%, respectively. This observation demonstrates the ability of
both methods to find high-quality, albeit different, solutions. The clas-
sical RSM slightly (yet consistently) outperforms the GRST in terms
of TAC, whereas the reliability comparison results are mixed with no
clear advantage for either method. Careful examination of the optimal
solutions reveals the substitutability of system components with others
to achieve a similar performance. For example, in the nominal problem
with $40/kWh penalty cost, the GRST solution used 3.7% fewer WT
than the classical RSM solution, but compensated for them by installing
6.9% more PV, 3.1% more BB capacity and 4.3% more DG capacity
to achieve almost the same TAC and reliability. This substitutability
explains why the problem might have multiple near-optimal, but very
different, solutions. Furthermore, it is clear that the GRST enjoys much
smaller computational times compared to the classical RSM when
implemented to the nominal problem, with savings that range between
48.9% and 64.9%. In contrast, this computational time advantage of
the GRST is inconclusive for the robust problem, perhaps because it
requires the min–max problem (20) to be solved in every iteration.
Based on the comparative analysis performed above, the main
advantage of the classical RSM over the GRST is its ability to find
slightly better solutions in terms of TAC, and sometimes also reliability.
However, its performance is found to be highly dependent on the
starting point and the design variables’ levels, i.e., R-III and CCD levels
and intervals. A starting point that is too far from optimal or improperly
set design levels might lead the search in a ‘‘wrong’’ direction based on
local information, thus ending at a local optimum. In other words, to
reach a near-optimal solution using the classical RSM, prior knowledge
about the system is needed. On the other hand, although the solutions
obtained using the GRST have marginally higher TAC values compared
to the classical RSM solutions, the computational times for the latter
are significantly smaller, especially in the nominal case. Furthermore,
the number of iterations can be controlled by the planner via setting
the initial search space and the stopping criterion (since the search
space is reduced by a predetermined factor in each iteration). Another
advantage of the GRST is that it uses global information from the

6. Conclusions and future research
Stand-alone HRES are generally more suitable than single-source
systems to supply power in off-grid applications, especially in remote
areas with difficult access. However, these systems must be designed
carefully and account for the stochasticity and uncertainty in supply
data to serve the demand at high reliability and affordable cost. In this
study, a stand-alone HRES that consists of PV panels and wind turbines,
integrated with battery storage and diesel generator, is considered to
implement a cost-minimization design approach. In order to capture un-
certainty in supply power, a finite number of scenarios with uncertain
probabilities are extracted from time-series data of both solar and wind
power through 𝑘-means clustering. Next, to tackle the uncertainty in
scenarios’ probability, an ambiguity set based on the Variation Distance
𝜙-divergence is constructed around the nominal probability of scenar-
ios. Since TAC and reliability functions cannot be evaluated explicitly,
two novel robust simulation–optimization methods, namely Classical
RSM and GRST, are proposed to estimate the objective function from
a surrogate model and optimize it. The presented methods are very
generic and flexible as they can be used for different applications,
and not only HRES design, with different objectives, operational rules,
reliability metrics, scenario generation methods, ambiguity sets, etc.
The numerical experiments conducted on a realistic case study have
shown the applicability and effectiveness of both methods. The optimal
designs obtained using the classical RSM were found to marginally
outperform the GRST designs in terms of TAC, whereas the reliabil-
ity comparison results were mixed. However, the GRST is faster to
